title: Red Feather Lakes Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Red Feather Lakes wells have a 250-foot median depth, with drilling and finished-well costs shaped by fractured mountain bedrock.
h1: Red Feather Lakes Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Red Feather Lakes means understanding how fractured mountain bedrock affects both water supply and construction cost. Within 5 miles, Colorado Division of Water Resources records show 1,660 permitted wells, with 1,248 recorded as constructed. The median well is 250 feet deep, but local results vary widely. A finished well at that depth may cost substantially more than the drilling alone because the project also includes the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and the records are concentrated in the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Nearby records from Red Fe Lks, Livermore, Bellvue, Glen Haven, Laporte, and Drake can help establish local expectations, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular lot.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Red Feather Lakes?
sections.html:
Recorded well depths around Red Feather Lakes have a 250-foot median. The middle half runs from 125 to 400 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss a large part of the local range. The 90th-percentile depth is 550 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 901 feet.

The depth mix shows why a driller needs room for uncertainty: 15% of wells are under 100 feet, 42% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 34% from 300 to 600 feet, and 9% are deeper than 600 feet. In fractured granite and gneiss, water is found in fractures rather than a predictable, uniform layer. Nearby wells are useful evidence, but the exact site geology still controls the final depth.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Red Feather Lakes well make?
sections.html:
The reported median pump yield is 4.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 7.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable household result for many homes when storage and system design are matched to the supply, but it is not the same as an abundant well.

Production is variable: 7% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, 46% produce from 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 44% from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 4% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Only 712 wells report a pump yield, so these figures should guide investigation rather than serve as a promise. Ask for the neighboring well permits, completion reports, and pump tests before relying on a specific lot.

sections.heading: What the water-level records show near Red Feather Lakes
sections.html:
Among the 103 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 87 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 31 to 100 feet. A water level at 87 feet does not tell you how much water the well will produce; it describes where the water stood when measured.

The decade series deserves attention. The median measured level was 25 feet below the surface in the 1980s, compared with 100 feet in the 2010s and 100 feet in the 2020s. That pattern suggests deeper measured water levels in the later records, although the sample is limited and measurements may come from different wells and conditions. Treat it as a reason to review current neighboring data, not as proof that every local water table is dropping.

sections.heading: Who has drilled wells here, and how active is the permit history?
sections.html:
Permit records extend from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. Activity was highest from the 1970s through the 1990s, with 340 permits in the 1970s, 310 in the 1980s, and 348 in the 1990s. The records also include 246 permits from the 2000s, 119 from the 2010s, and 66 from the 2020s.

The most common drillers in these records are Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.), Hersh & Son Well Drilling Inc (Hersh, Harry), and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed). These names show local permit history, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, the proposed casing and grout design, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Red Feather Lakes?
sections.html:
Local drilling is modeled for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65-$100 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $16,200-$25,000. That is not the complete water-system price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $22,200-$37,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move beyond that range, while a shallower hole may not reduce every fixed project cost. Request an itemized bid showing drilling, casing, grout, pump installation, storage, trenching, electrical work, testing, and permit-related work. In this bedrock setting, also ask how the contract handles additional footage and an unsuccessful or low-yield hole.

sections.heading: Risks to investigate before building or buying
sections.html:
Low yield is the most direct water-supply concern. The records include 7% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and fractured rock can change sharply from one property to the next. Dry holes and deeper-than-expected drilling are possible, so a neighboring well review should be part of due diligence.

There are 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 12 historic mine features mapped within about 10 miles. No EPA Superfund or cleanup sites are mapped in that area, but that does not replace a property-specific water test. Test for appropriate local concerns and review the well construction record. Confirm septic setbacks, available building areas, driveway access, and separation between the well and septic system before purchasing or placing a home. Most local permits are domestic or household use, so confirm the permitted use matches your plans.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Red Feather Lakes is 250 feet. The middle half ranges from 125 to 400 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 550 feet. Records range from under 100 feet to a deepest recorded well of 901 feet, reflecting variable fractured mountain bedrock.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65-$100 per foot. At the 250-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $16,200-$25,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $22,200-$37,000. A driller should explain how deeper footage or a low-yield hole changes the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 4.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Seven percent of reported wells produce under 1 gallon per minute. Since only 712 wells report yield, review nearby completion reports and pump tests rather than relying on the area median alone.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: Well safety cannot be determined from depth or yield. Records map 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 12 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped. Test the specific well, review its construction and history, and consider site conditions near mines, septic systems, and other potential sources.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Red Feather Lakes?
faq.a: Check the DWR permit, construction report, depth, pump yield, static water level, and permitted use. Nearby records show a 250-foot median depth and 4.0-gallon-per-minute median yield, but individual results vary. Also confirm septic and building locations, driveway access, water testing, and the cost of replacing or upgrading the well system.
